US seasonal hiring is off to a weak start:

US-based employers announced plans to hire 90,787 workers in September, the weakest September total since 2011.

This marks a -23% decline from the 117,313 recorded in September 2025.

Retail led all industries last month, with 65,150 announced hires, followed by Aerospace and Defense at 5,300.

However, announced seasonal hiring is muted so far this year, with a combined 62,000 seasonal hires, compared with 100,800 announced by seasonal employers last September.

Year-to-date, US hiring plans have totaled 210,612 workers, the 2nd-lowest total for the first 9 months of the year in at least 10 years.

Retail leads all sectors with 66,557 announcements so far in 2026, followed by Technology, at 22,361, and Aerospace and Defense, at 21,841.

Hiring demand remains muted.

Powerful quantum computers could pose a serious risk.

And preparing the world's infrastructure for quantum attacks will take longer than most people expect.

I came across this breakdown from @PaloAltoNtwks, and it got me thinking about how many systems we'd actually need to upgrade.

We're talking about:

→ Payment systems
→ Digital identities and authentication
→ Software updates and security checks
→ Older connected devices that may be difficult to update

With so much infrastructure to upgrade, I can see why NIST isn't waiting around. It finalized its first three quantum-resistant cryptography standards in 2024 and is already urging organizations to adopt them.

There's another concern, too.

Encrypted data stolen today could become readable years later, once quantum computers become powerful enough.

Lots of ground to cover, so best start early if you ask me.

Very excited tbh.

🌎🚨 Bond markets are starting to do central banks' job for them as investors have priced out nearly 180 basis points of expected rate hikes across eight major economies.

📉 Rising bond yields are tightening financial conditions without central banks having to intervene. Households face higher borrowing costs, companies have to finance their investments at less favorable rates, and governments are gradually seeing their refinancing costs increase. All of this weighs on economic activity and could therefore reduce the need for central banks to raise policy rates further. The cumulative rate hikes expected over the next 12 months across eight economies have fallen from 717 to 539 basis points since September.

⚠️ However, not all increases in long-term yields are created equal. If yields are rising because the economy is strong or investors expect persistent inflation, that's one thing, but if they're rising because markets are demanding higher risk premiums to finance government deficits, that's a different story. Right now, we're dealing with a combination of both. Between massive US deficits, concerns over France's public finances, enormous AI-related financing needs and the energy shock triggered by the conflict with Iran, the pressure on long-term yields goes well beyond monetary policy. I believe the risk is that central banks stop raising rates, or even start cutting them, without financial conditions actually improving.

➡️ There is another thing that I believe is fundamental. If long-term yields keep climbing despite policy rates stabilizing, we could see renewed discussions around slowing QT, Operation Twist-style interventions, or outright bond purchases. None of this is inevitable or necessarily desirable as intervening to suppress yields while inflation remains elevated could undermine monetary credibility and fuel even higher risk premiums.

For years, markets were mainly worried about central banks tightening financial conditions too aggressively, but now the risk is that they may no longer be able to ease financial conditions sufficiently, even when they want to.

One of my more controversial bets: the AI feed will be the form factor of 2027!

Most people don’t know what to prompt, and they won’t prompt their way into complicated agentic workflows. With chat, we ask users for digital labor: figure out what AI can do, explain the task, provide the context, repeat. That’s a lot to ask if we want billions of people using agents every day. 

Meanwhile, people already spend hours in feeds. Twitter, Instagram, LinkedIn. They know how to scroll, discover something useful, and act on it.

An intelligent system that knows you should bring you the next useful action. Here’s the email you need to answer, already drafted. Here are the latest sales numbers, with an update ready to send to your team. You approve, edit, dismiss, or jump into chat to go deeper. That’s how people will discover what agents can do, without having to invent a prompt first.

And you can put ads in a feed, one of the biggest business models on the internet. A system that understands your plans can recommend a relevant restaurant, product, or service, clearly labeled as sponsored. You get a reason to come back every day, useful work ready to approve, and a business model to fund the agents doing it.

Meanwhile, people already spend hours in feeds. Twitter, Instagram, LinkedIn. They know how to scroll, discover something useful, and act on it.

An intelligent system that knows you should bring you the next useful action. Here’s the email you need to answer, already drafted. Here are the latest sales numbers, with an update ready to send to your team. You approve, edit, dismiss, or jump into chat to go deeper. That’s how people will discover what agents can do, without having to invent a prompt first.

And you can put ads in a feed, one of the biggest business models on the internet. A system that understands your plans can recommend a relevant restaurant, product, or service, clearly labeled as sponsored. You get a reason to come back every day, useful work ready to approve, and a business model to fund the agents doing it.

The real SaaS apocalypse is pretty simple: every piece of software becomes reproducible. The cost of building it goes toward zero, competition becomes brutal, and eventually the price follows. Good luck charging for something anyone can recreate.

Computer use is the breakthrough here imo. Here’s how it works:

One agent navigates the existing software, clicks through every feature and documents everything in a markdown file. A swarm of agents builds it. Another agent acts as the verifier, opens the new software, clicks everywhere, checks that everything works, sends bugs back. Repeat.

I think this scenario is very possible and very much in the work. 

But people are missing the other side which is the bull case for big tech cos. 

If you’re Adobe, you already have a massive test suite documenting how the software is supposed to behave, including all the backend stuff you can’t discover by clicking around. You have insane usage telemetry, decades of customer feedback, and you know which obscure features people actually depend on.

You can build the same software factory. Except you start with a huge advantage.

Use the agents to clean up decades of legacy code. Make the software load faster, feel faster, break less. Give it clean APIs that agents can use. Then use your distribution to ship that better product to millions of existing customers.

Even if you burn $1M in tokens doing this, that’s roughly the annual cost of a handful of engineers in the Bay Area.

And getting the mass market to switch takes time. Especially in the enterprise. A free open-source alternative still has to earn trust, build credibility and convince people to move their workflows. “We cloned Photoshop” doesn’t automatically do that.

So there’s also a pretty strong bull case: the incumbents build the software factory first, use their tests, customer knowledge and distribution to move faster, and end up with better software, higher margins, more revenue and happier customers.

If they don’t move fast enough, well, we’re back to the bear case.
